Chapter 1  ·  Machine Learning Foundations

Linear Classifiers
and Decision Boundaries

From sample points and feature spaces to hyperplanes, normal vectors, and the geometry of linear separation.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish features, labels, and sample points, and represent observations as vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$.
  • Define a decision function $f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ and derive its associated decision boundary as an isosurface.
  • State the geometric properties of hyperplanes—dimension, flatness, and the role of the normal vector $\mathbf{w}$.
  • Compute signed distance from a point to a hyperplane when $\mathbf{w}$ is a unit vector, and interpret its sign geometrically.
  • Derive and implement the centroid method for binary linear classification, including the closed-form formula for $\alpha$.
  • Explain linear separability and identify when a linear classifier cannot achieve zero training error.
  • Identify overfitting by connecting decision-boundary complexity to validation performance.
  • Formulate the perceptron as a gradient-descent optimizer on a piecewise-linear loss, and describe its convergence guarantee.

1.1 Feature Spaces and Classification

Machine learning begins with observations. Each observation is a collection of measurable attributes—called features—together with a quantity we want to predict, called the label. The distinction between features and labels is conceptually simple but easy to blur in practice: features are the inputs available at prediction time, while the label is what we would like to infer.

As a running example throughout this chapter, consider predicting whether a person prefers chocolate ice cream to vanilla given only their height and age. Here the features are height and age, and the label is binary: does the person prefer chocolate, or not? Neither height nor age is the object of prediction—they are the inputs we use to guess the object of prediction. This separation is the defining structure of supervised learning.

Once we have identified features, we immediately gain a powerful tool: geometry. Each feature defines an axis of a coordinate system, and every observation becomes a point in that coordinate system. This geometric viewpoint is not merely a visualization trick—it is the conceptual foundation on which all of the algorithms in this course are built.

1.1.1 Features, Labels, and Sample Points

Definition · Feature Space and Sample Points

Let $d \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ be the number of features. The feature space is $\mathbb{R}^d$. A sample point (also called a feature vector or, in regression contexts, an independent variable) is a vector $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ whose $j$-th component $x_j$ records the value of the $j$-th feature for that observation. A label is a value $y$ drawn from a label set $\mathcal{Y}$; for binary classification, $\mathcal{Y} = \{-1,+1\}$ or $\mathcal{Y} = \{0,1\}$. A training set of size $n$ is a set of labeled pairs $\{(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^n$, with $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $y_i \in \mathcal{Y}$.

Throughout this course we use $n$ for the number of sample points and $d$ for the dimension of the feature space. These two letters are reserved: you will almost never see $n$ used for anything else, nor $d$ used to mean anything other than dimension. This consistency is deliberate—when reading a formula, recognizing $n$ and $d$ immediately tells you whether you are counting observations or features.

Intuition · Why Geometric Thinking Works

Think of each feature as a ruler measuring one aspect of an observation. Two features give you a flat table; three give you a room; $d$ features give you a $d$-dimensional space your physical intuition cannot directly visualize, but whose algebra behaves identically. The point is that similarity in feature space approximates similarity in the real world: observations that are close together tend to share the same label. Classification algorithms exploit this by drawing boundaries between regions of feature space.

1.1.2 Decision Boundaries and Overfitting

Given a training set, a binary classifier partitions feature space into two regions: a region it labels $+1$ (class $\mathcal{C}$) and a region it labels $-1$ (not class $\mathcal{C}$). The surface separating these two regions is the decision boundary. Different classifiers produce decision boundaries of different shapes—lines, circles, complicated wiggly curves—and the art of machine learning consists partly in choosing the right shape for each problem.

Consider three scenarios illustrated in Figure 1.1. In the first, the chocolate lovers and vanilla lovers cluster cleanly on opposite sides of a straight line. In the second, the classes form concentric rings—no straight line works, but a circle does. In the third, the points are scattered unpredictably; a sinuous curve can thread through every training point and achieve zero training error, but almost certainly at the cost of failing to generalize.

Figure 1.1. Three binary classification scenarios in a 2D feature space (height on $x_1$, age on $x_2$). Left: the two classes are linearly separable; the green line achieves zero training error. Center: a circular (quadratic) boundary in green separates concentrically distributed classes. Right: a sinuous red dashed curve achieves zero training error but almost certainly overfits. Blue circles = chocolate preference; gold squares = vanilla preference.
Definition · Decision Boundary and Overfitting

The decision boundary of a classifier is the set of points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ at which the classifier changes its prediction from class $\mathcal{C}$ to not-$\mathcal{C}$. A classifier overfits if its decision boundary fits spurious detail in the training data—patterns not reproducible in new data—causing its performance on held-out validation points to deteriorate relative to a simpler boundary, even one that makes some training errors.

Warning · Training Error Is Not Validation Error

Zero training error is not evidence of a good classifier; it is evidence only that the classifier has enough parameters to memorize the training data. The correct diagnostic is validation error: how well does the classifier predict labels for observations it has never seen? Only validation error—not training error—tells you whether you have overfit. Never select models, hyperparameters, or decision boundaries based on training performance alone.

1.2 Decision Functions and Isosurfaces

Most classifiers in this course do not specify a decision boundary directly. Instead, they define a scalar-valued function over the entire feature space—a decision function—whose sign determines the prediction at any point. The decision boundary then emerges automatically as the set of points where this function equals zero. This indirect approach is powerful because it replaces the geometric problem of drawing a boundary with the analytic problem of optimizing a function.

Understanding why the zero-set of a function is a useful boundary requires some familiarity with isosurfaces—a concept from analysis that generalizes contour lines to arbitrary dimensions. Just as the contour lines of a topographic map trace paths of equal altitude, the isosurfaces of a decision function trace sets of equal predicted score. The zero-isosurface is the decision boundary; other isosurfaces convey how confident the classifier is about its prediction.

1.2.1 Decision Functions

Definition · Decision Function

A decision function for a binary classification problem is a function $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$. The classifier predicts class $\mathcal{C}$ for a point $\mathbf{x}$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) > 0$, and predicts not-$\mathcal{C}$ if $f(\mathbf{x}) \leq 0$. In the literature, decision functions are also called predictor functions or discriminant functions.

The associated decision boundary is the zero-level set: $$\mathcal{H} = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d : f(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}.$$

The choice of zero as the threshold is conventional rather than essential. There are circumstances in which it is useful to use a non-zero iso-value—for example, when the costs of the two types of error differ—but in this chapter we use the convention $f(\mathbf{x}) = 0$ as the boundary.

Example · A Radial Decision Function

Setup. Consider the decision function $f(x_1, x_2) = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2} - 3$ in two-dimensional feature space.

Analysis. The decision boundary is the set where $f = 0$, i.e., $\sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2} = 3$: a circle of radius 3 centered at the origin. Inside the circle ($f < 0$) the classifier predicts class $\mathcal{C}$; outside ($f > 0$) it predicts not-$\mathcal{C}$.

Isosurface family. Every level set $\{f = c\}$ is a circle of radius $c + 3$, defined for $c > -3$. The minimum of $f$ is $-3$ at the origin, where the "confidence" of the inside-class prediction is highest. This is not a linear classifier—the boundary is curved—but it illustrates the general principle perfectly.

1.2.2 Isosurfaces and Level Sets

Definition · Isosurface

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$. The isosurface (or level set) of $f$ at value $c$ is $$S_c(f) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d : f(\mathbf{x}) = c\}.$$ Generically, $S_c(f)$ is a $(d-1)$-dimensional surface in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The gradient $\nabla f(\mathbf{x})$ is always orthogonal to the isosurface passing through $\mathbf{x}$ (when $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}) \neq \mathbf{0}$).

The connection between gradient and isosurface is fundamental. Because the gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent of $f$, and isosurfaces are surfaces along which $f$ is constant, the gradient must be perpendicular to any direction along the isosurface. This geometric fact will be crucial in Section 1.4 when we interpret the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ of a linear classifier as a normal to the decision boundary.

Figure 1.2. Two representations of $f(x_1,x_2) = \sqrt{x_1^2+x_2^2} - 3$. Left: 3D surface plot; the cone shape has its minimum at the origin. Right: isocontour plot; each ring is a level set $S_c(f)$ for $c = -3,-2,-1,0,1,2$. Shaded blue = class $\mathcal{C}$ ($f < 0$). The zero contour (green) is the circular decision boundary of radius 3. Gradient vectors would point radially outward, perpendicular to all contours.
Intuition · Reading an Isocontour Plot

An isocontour plot is a map of a scalar function’s terrain. Where contours are closely spaced, the function changes value quickly—the gradient is large. Where they are widely spaced, the function changes slowly. The decision boundary (zero contour) separates the "positive side" from the "negative side," just as a mountain ridge separates two valleys. When you look at a classifier’s isocontour plot, you can immediately read off which region is predicted as class $\mathcal{C}$ and how confident the classifier is as you move away from the boundary.

💡
Key insight: The decision boundary of a classifier is just one isosurface among infinitely many. Every other isosurface encodes the classifier’s confidence—how far a point is from the boundary. In Section 1.4, this becomes the signed distance interpretation of linear decision functions.
Data Science Application · Confidence Scores and Calibration

In production ML systems, it is rarely enough to output a binary prediction. A model that predicts class $\mathcal{C}$ with $f(\mathbf{x}) = 0.001$ is much less reliable than one with $f(\mathbf{x}) = 10$, even though both produce the same binary output. The magnitude $|f(\mathbf{x})|$ is a raw confidence score—large values indicate the point is far from the boundary, small values indicate ambiguity. Calibration (converting raw scores to well-calibrated probabilities via isotonic regression or Platt scaling) is a standard post-processing step in practice.

1.3 Vector Notation and Inner Products

Because all of our sample points, weight vectors, and parameters live in $\mathbb{R}^d$, a precise and consistent notation for vectors is essential. Confusion about whether a vector is a row or a column, or whether an expression is a scalar or a matrix, is a perennial source of errors in machine learning derivations. This section establishes the conventions we use throughout the course.

The most important computational tool is the dot product (also called the inner product). Almost every linear classifier reduces, at its core, to a dot product: the classification score for a point $\mathbf{x}$ is $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha$, where $\mathbf{w}$ is a weight vector and $\alpha$ is a scalar bias. Understanding dot products geometrically—not just as a formula—is what allows us to interpret classifiers, prove theorems about them, and design better ones.

1.3.1 Notation Conventions

Definition · Notation Conventions
  • Vectors are written as lowercase boldface letters ($\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \boldsymbol{\mu}$) and are assumed to be column vectors $\in \mathbb{R}^d$ unless stated otherwise.
  • Matrices are written as uppercase roman letters ($X, W, \Sigma$).
  • Random variables also use uppercase roman letters ($X, Y$); context determines whether a capital letter is a matrix or a random variable.
  • Scalars use lowercase Greek letters ($\alpha, \beta, \lambda$) or lowercase roman letters ($n, d, i, j, k$).
  • The integers $n$ (number of sample points) and $d$ (number of features) are reserved throughout the course.
  • Indices $i, j, k$ appear only in subscripts of sums or sequences; they are never vectors.
  • Functions are written $f(\mathbf{x})$, $s(\mathbf{x})$, etc., and are scalar-valued unless noted.

1.3.2 Dot Products, Norms, and Angles

Definition · Euclidean Inner Product, Norm, and Angle

For $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the Euclidean inner product (dot product) is $$\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{x}^\top \mathbf{y} = \sum_{j=1}^d x_j y_j.$$ The Euclidean norm is $\|\mathbf{x}\| = \sqrt{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{x}} = \bigl(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. The unit vector in the direction of $\mathbf{x} \neq \mathbf{0}$ is $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x}/\|\mathbf{x}\|$; this operation is called normalizing $\mathbf{x}$.

For $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \neq \mathbf{0}$, the angle $\theta \in [0, \pi]$ between them satisfies $$\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|\,\|\mathbf{y}\|}.$$ Consequently: $\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} > 0$ iff $\theta < \pi/2$ (acute); $\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} = 0$ iff $\theta = \pi/2$ (orthogonal); $\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{y} < 0$ iff $\theta > \pi/2$ (obtuse).

Linear Decision Function
$$f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + \alpha$$

This expression—a dot product plus a scalar—is the canonical form of a linear decision function. The vector $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (the weight vector) and the scalar $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ (the bias) together determine the classifier. Learning a linear classifier means choosing $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$ that produce good predictions. These are also called parameters or, in regression contexts, regression coefficients. The name "weights" reflects that each component $w_j$ tells us how heavily the $j$-th feature is weighted in the classification decision.

Example · Computing a Dot Product and Orthogonality

Setup. Let $d = 3$, $\mathbf{w} = (1, 2, -1)^\top$, $\mathbf{x} = (3, 0, 1)^\top$, $\mathbf{y} = (2, -1, 4)^\top$.

Computation. $$\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = (1)(3) + (2)(0) + (-1)(1) = 2, \qquad \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{y} = (1)(2) + (2)(-1) + (-1)(4) = -4.$$ $$\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot (1, 1, -3)^\top = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 \neq 0.$$

Interpretation. Since $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = 2 > 0$, the classifier (with $\alpha = 0$) predicts class $\mathcal{C}$ for $\mathbf{x}$. Since $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{y} = -4 < 0$, it predicts not-$\mathcal{C}$ for $\mathbf{y}$. The fact that $\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}) \neq 0$ means the vector connecting $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ is not tangent to the decision boundary. We will see in Section 1.4 that any vector lying in the boundary must be orthogonal to $\mathbf{w}$.

1.4 Hyperplanes and Normal Vectors

The most important class of decision boundaries for this course is the class of hyperplanes—the zero-level sets of linear decision functions. Hyperplanes generalize lines (in $\mathbb{R}^2$) and planes (in $\mathbb{R}^3$) to arbitrary dimensions, inheriting three characteristic properties: they have one fewer dimension than the ambient space, they are flat, and they are infinite.

The key structural result of this section is that the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ in a linear decision function is normal to the hyperplane—perpendicular to every direction lying in it. This seemingly simple fact has profound consequences: $\mathbf{w}$ encodes the orientation of the boundary, while $\alpha$ encodes its position. Changing $\mathbf{w}$ tilts the boundary; changing $\alpha$ translates it without rotation. And when $\mathbf{w}$ is normalized to unit length, the value $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha$ becomes exactly the signed perpendicular distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to the hyperplane.

1.4.1 Hyperplane Geometry

Definition · Hyperplane

A hyperplane in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is any set of the form $$\mathcal{H} = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d : \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha = 0\}$$ for some fixed $\mathbf{w} \in \mathbb{R}^d \setminus \{\mathbf{0}\}$ and $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Three geometric properties characterize hyperplanes:

  • Dimension $d-1$: $\mathcal{H}$ is a $(d-1)$-dimensional affine subspace of $\mathbb{R}^d$, cutting the space into exactly two open half-spaces.
  • Flatness: Any line segment between two points of $\mathcal{H}$ lies entirely in $\mathcal{H}$.
  • Infinite extent: $\mathcal{H}$ is unbounded in all directions within its affine span.

In $d=2$ a hyperplane is a line; in $d=3$ it is a plane; in $d=1$ it degenerates to a single point.

The parameter $\alpha$ is called the bias of the hyperplane. When $\alpha = 0$, the hyperplane passes through the origin. When $\alpha \neq 0$, the hyperplane is translated away from the origin by an amount we will quantify in Section 1.4.3. This is why, in the centroid method and the perceptron, we must explicitly learn $\alpha$ as well as $\mathbf{w}$—without it, our classifier would be forced to use only hyperplanes through the origin, a severe restriction.

Figure 1.3. A family of parallel hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^2$, all sharing the same normal vector $\mathbf{w} = (1,1)^\top/\sqrt{2}$ (red arrow). The four lines correspond to $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = c$ for $c = -1, 0, 1, 2$. Changing $c$ (equivalently, changing $\alpha$) translates the line along the $\mathbf{w}$ direction without rotating it.

1.4.2 The Normal Vector Theorem

We now prove the central geometric fact about linear decision functions: the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$ is perpendicular (normal) to the hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$.

Theorem · Normal Vector of a Hyperplane

Let $\mathcal{H} = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d : \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha = 0\}$ be a hyperplane. For any two points $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{H}$, $$\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) = 0.$$ That is, $\mathbf{w}$ is orthogonal to every vector lying in $\mathcal{H}$, and is therefore called the normal vector of $\mathcal{H}$.

Proof

Since $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{H}$, by definition $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha = 0$ and $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{y} + \alpha = 0$, so $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = -\alpha$ and $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{y} = -\alpha$. Therefore $$\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} = (-\alpha) - (-\alpha) = 0. \qquad \square$$ □

The theorem says $\mathbf{w}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}$ for any two points in $\mathcal{H}$. Since these difference vectors span the entire $(d-1)$-dimensional tangent space of $\mathcal{H}$, $\mathbf{w}$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal{H}$ in every direction. This is also why we named the weight vector $\mathbf{w}$: it is normal (another word for perpendicular) to the hyperplane it defines.

ℹ️
Connection to gradients: For a linear function $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha$, the gradient is $\nabla f = \mathbf{w}$ (constant everywhere). The fact that the gradient is orthogonal to isosurfaces (mentioned in Section 1.2.2) immediately implies the Normal Vector Theorem as a special case.

1.4.3 Signed Distance Interpretation

Theorem · Signed Distance Formula

Suppose $\|\mathbf{w}\| = 1$. Then for any $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$, the value $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha$ equals the signed perpendicular distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to the hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$: $$\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{H}) = |f(\mathbf{x})| = |\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha|.$$ The sign of $f(\mathbf{x})$ is positive on the side toward which $\mathbf{w}$ points, negative on the opposite side. The distance from the origin to $\mathcal{H}$ is $|\alpha|$.

Proof

Let $\mathbf{x}_0$ be the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\mathcal{H}$. Since $\mathbf{w}$ is normal to $\mathcal{H}$, we have $\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0 = t\mathbf{w}$ for some scalar $t$, and $\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{H}) = |t|$. Since $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \mathcal{H}$, $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + \alpha = 0$. Then: $$f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{x}_0 + t\mathbf{w}) + \alpha = (\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_0 + \alpha) + t\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 = 0 + t \cdot 1 = t.$$ Hence $f(\mathbf{x}) = t$ and $\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{H}) = |t| = |f(\mathbf{x})|$. Setting $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ gives $f(\mathbf{0}) = \alpha$, so the signed distance from the origin to $\mathcal{H}$ is $\alpha$. □

When $\mathbf{w}$ is not a unit vector (as is common in practice), we can always rescale: divide both $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$ by $\|\mathbf{w}\|$. The rescaled equation defines the same hyperplane but now the weight vector is a unit vector, restoring the signed-distance interpretation. This rescaling is equivalent to computing $\mathrm{dist}(\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{H}) = |\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha| / \|\mathbf{w}\|$ without explicitly normalizing.

Figure 1.4. Signed distance in $\mathbb{R}^2$. The hyperplane $\mathcal{H}$ (black line) satisfies $x_1 + x_2 = 2$, with unit normal $\mathbf{w} = (1,1)^\top/\sqrt{2}$ (blue arrow). Shaded blue region: $f > 0$ (w-side); shaded red region: $f < 0$ (opposite side). Dashed arrows show perpendicular distances from labeled points to $\mathcal{H}$: A (blue dot, $f > 0$) is on the w-side; B (red dot, $f < 0$) is on the other side; C (green dot, $f = 0$) lies on $\mathcal{H}$. Arrow lengths equal $|f|$ since $\mathbf{w}$ is a unit vector.
Example · Signed Distance Computation

Setup. Let $\mathbf{w} = (3, 4)^\top$ (not a unit vector) and $\alpha = -5$. The hyperplane is $3x_1 + 4x_2 - 5 = 0$. Compute the distance from $\mathbf{x} = (2, 2)^\top$ to this hyperplane.

Step 1: Normalize. $\|\mathbf{w}\| = \sqrt{9+16} = 5$. Unit normal: $\hat{\mathbf{w}} = (3/5, 4/5)^\top$, normalized bias: $\hat{\alpha} = -1$.

Step 2: Evaluate. $f(\mathbf{x}) = (3/5)(2) + (4/5)(2) - 1 = 6/5 + 8/5 - 1 = 14/5 - 5/5 = 9/5$.

Result. The signed distance is $9/5 = 1.8$. The point $(2,2)^\top$ is 1.8 units from the hyperplane, on the $\mathbf{w}$-side. Verification: $f(\mathbf{x}) = 3(2)+4(2)-5 = 9$; dividing by $\|\mathbf{w}\| = 5$ gives $9/5 = 1.8$. ✓

1.5 The Centroid Method

Having established the geometry of linear classifiers, we are ready to study our first complete algorithm: the centroid method. The centroid method is not the best linear classifier available (we will see better ones in later chapters), but it is analytically tractable, geometrically transparent, and requires no iterative optimization. It also introduces the idea of using class statistics—means, in this case—to design decision boundaries, a strategy that reappears in more sophisticated methods such as linear discriminant analysis.

The key question the centroid method answers is: given only the class means, what is the most natural linear boundary between the two classes? The answer is the hyperplane that perpendicularly bisects the segment connecting the two class centroids. This boundary is intuitive—it is equidistant from both class means—and it is computable in closed form from the training data without any optimization.

1.5.1 Algorithm and Derivation

Definition · Class Centroids

Given a training set for binary classification with class $\mathcal{C}$ and complement $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$, define the class centroids: $$\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|} \sum_{i:\, y_i = +1} \mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}} = \frac{1}{|\overline{\mathcal{C}}|} \sum_{i:\, y_i = -1} \mathbf{x}_i.$$ Each centroid is the component-wise mean of the feature vectors in that class.

Centroid Classifier
$$f(\mathbf{x}) = (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}) \cdot \mathbf{x} - (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}) \cdot \frac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}}{2}$$
Theorem · Centroid Classifier is a Perpendicular Bisector

Define $\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$ and $\alpha = -\mathbf{w} \cdot \tfrac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}}{2}$. Then the hyperplane $\mathcal{H} = \{f = 0\}$ satisfies: (1) the midpoint $\mathbf{m} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}})$ lies in $\mathcal{H}$; (2) $\mathbf{w}$ is normal to $\mathcal{H}$ and parallel to $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$. Hence $\mathcal{H}$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment $[\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}}, \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}]$.

Proof

For (1): $f(\mathbf{m}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{m} + \alpha = \mathbf{w} \cdot \tfrac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}}{2} - \mathbf{w} \cdot \tfrac{\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} + \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}}{2} = 0$. ✓

For (2): $\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$ is normal to $\mathcal{H}$ by the Normal Vector Theorem (Section 1.4.2). This vector is also the direction from $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$ to $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}}$. A hyperplane through the midpoint of a segment, normal to that segment, is its perpendicular bisector by definition. ✓ □

1.5.2 Geometric Interpretation

The centroid method can be described as a nearest-centroid rule: a point $\mathbf{x}$ is classified as $\mathcal{C}$ if and only if it is closer to $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}}$ than to $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$ (in terms of the projection onto the inter-centroid axis). This geometric description makes the algorithm easy to understand, implement, and analyze.

Figure 1.5. The centroid method in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Blue circles: class $\mathcal{C}$ (chocolate); gold squares: class $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ (vanilla). Stars mark the centroids $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}}$ (blue) and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$ (gold); the green diamond is the midpoint $\mathbf{m}$. The red arrow is the weight vector $\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$. The green line is the decision boundary (perpendicular bisector). Note that several training points are misclassified: the centroid method does not minimize training error.
Intuition · When Centroid Method Fails

The centroid method is optimal (in the Bayes sense) when both classes follow Gaussian distributions with equal covariance matrices and equal priors. When those assumptions fail—as they usually do—the centroid method may underperform. In particular, it ignores the spread of each class: a tight cluster near one centroid and a diffuse cloud around the other will confuse it, because it treats all training points equally regardless of their distance from the centroid.

Data Science Application · Rocchio Algorithm for Text Classification

The centroid method applied to TF-IDF feature vectors is known as the Rocchio algorithm in information retrieval. Each document is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ (vocabulary size), and the centroid of the "sports" class is a vector with high weight on sports-related words. New documents are classified by comparing their TF-IDF vectors to the two class centroids. Rocchio is fast (no iteration), interpretable (the centroid is the "average document" for that class), and competitive for short-text classification tasks where the Gaussian assumption is approximately satisfied.

1.6 The Perceptron Algorithm

The centroid method gives us a closed-form classifier requiring no iteration. But the approach we will use for most of this course is fundamentally different: we will define an objective function—a measure of how wrong our current classifier is—and then minimize it iteratively. This paradigm, known as empirical risk minimization, is the engine of nearly all modern machine learning.

The perceptron, invented by Frank Rosenblatt in 1957, was the first algorithm to implement this paradigm for linear classification. Although superseded by faster and more powerful methods, the perceptron remains important: it introduces gradient descent in a crisp, analyzable setting; it is the historical ancestor of neural networks; and its convergence theorem provides one of the first rigorous performance guarantees in machine learning.

We study the perceptron not because it is the best linear classifier, but because it reveals the structure of gradient descent for classification problems in the simplest possible form—before we apply these ideas to logistic regression, SVMs, and neural networks.

1.6.1 Formulation and Labels

Definition · Perceptron Label Convention and Margin

The perceptron uses the $\{-1, +1\}$ label convention: $y_i = +1$ if $\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathcal{C}$, $y_i = -1$ otherwise. A training point $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$ is correctly classified by $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha$ iff $y_i \cdot f(\mathbf{x}_i) > 0$, and is misclassified iff $y_i \cdot f(\mathbf{x}_i) \leq 0$. The product $y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)$ is called the margin of point $i$ under the current classifier.

Definition · Perceptron Loss Function

The perceptron loss on the training set is $$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, \alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^n \max\bigl(0,\, -y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha)\bigr).$$ This sums $-y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) > 0$ only over misclassified points. When all points are correctly classified, $\mathcal{L} = 0$. The loss is piecewise linear and measures how badly each misclassified point is misclassified.

1.6.2 Gradient Descent and the Update Rule

Theorem · Perceptron Gradient and Update Rule

The gradient of the perceptron loss $\mathcal{L}$ with respect to the weights is: $$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{w}} = -\sum_{i:\, y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) \leq 0} y_i \mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \alpha} = -\sum_{i:\, y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) \leq 0} y_i.$$ A gradient-descent step with learning rate $\eta > 0$ gives the perceptron update rule: for each misclassified point $(\mathbf{x}_i, y_i)$, $$\boxed{\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta\, y_i \mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \alpha \leftarrow \alpha + \eta\, y_i.}$$

Proof

For a misclassified point $i$ where $y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) \leq 0$, the loss contribution is $\ell_i = -y_i(\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}_i + \alpha)$. This is linear in $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$, so: $$\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} \ell_i = -y_i \mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \frac{\partial \ell_i}{\partial \alpha} = -y_i.$$ Gradient descent steps in the $-\nabla$ direction, so $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta \sum_{\text{mis}} y_i \mathbf{x}_i$. In the classic perceptron, $\eta = 1$ and updates are applied stochastically, one point at a time. □

The update has a clean geometric interpretation: when a class-$+1$ point $\mathbf{x}_i$ is misclassified (on the negative side of the boundary), adding $y_i \mathbf{x}_i = \mathbf{x}_i$ to $\mathbf{w}$ rotates the boundary toward $\mathbf{x}_i$. When a class-$-1$ point is misclassified, subtracting $\mathbf{x}_i$ rotates the boundary away from it. In both cases, the update pushes the boundary to correctly classify that point—though it may simultaneously misclassify previously correct points.

Figure 1.6. Gradient descent on a simplified quadratic surrogate of the perceptron loss (for illustration). Left: Loss contours in $(w_1, w_2)$ space; the red path shows 18 gradient-descent steps from $(-2.5, 2.5)$ (gold dot), converging to the minimum (green star). Right: Loss versus iteration, showing monotonic decrease. In the actual perceptron (piecewise-linear loss, online updates), convergence is guaranteed in finite steps for linearly separable data but loss need not decrease at every step.
Figure 1.7. A single perceptron update step. Left (Before): A class-$+1$ point (red-bordered star) is misclassified; the current boundary (red dashed) has $\mathbf{w}$ (red arrow) pointing away from the misclassified point. Right (After): After adding $\eta y_i \mathbf{x}_i$ to $\mathbf{w}$, the boundary (green line) rotates and now correctly classifies the point (green-bordered star). In $\mathbb{R}^d$ the boundary is a hyperplane.

1.6.3 Convergence

Theorem · Perceptron Convergence (Novikoff, 1963)

Suppose the training set is linearly separable: there exists $\mathbf{w}^* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\|\mathbf{w}^*\| = 1$ and $\gamma > 0$ such that $y_i(\mathbf{w}^* \cdot \mathbf{x}_i) \geq \gamma$ for all $i$. Let $R = \max_i \|\mathbf{x}_i\|$. Then the perceptron algorithm makes at most $$\boxed{\frac{R^2}{\gamma^2}}$$ mistakes before finding a separating hyperplane.

Proof Sketch

Let $\mathbf{w}_k$ be the weight vector after $k$ mistakes (starting from $\mathbf{w}_0 = \mathbf{0}$). We track two quantities. First, each update increases the inner product with the optimal weight: $\mathbf{w}_k \cdot \mathbf{w}^* = \mathbf{w}_{k-1} \cdot \mathbf{w}^* + y_i(\mathbf{w}^* \cdot \mathbf{x}_i) \geq \mathbf{w}_{k-1} \cdot \mathbf{w}^* + \gamma$, so $\mathbf{w}_k \cdot \mathbf{w}^* \geq k\gamma$. Second, a mistake occurs only when $y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i) \leq 0$, and one can show $\|\mathbf{w}_k\|^2 \leq \|\mathbf{w}_{k-1}\|^2 + R^2$, giving $\|\mathbf{w}_k\|^2 \leq kR^2$. Combining via Cauchy-Schwarz: $k\gamma \leq \mathbf{w}_k \cdot \mathbf{w}^* \leq \|\mathbf{w}_k\|\|\mathbf{w}^*\| = \|\mathbf{w}_k\| \leq \sqrt{k}\,R$. Squaring: $k^2\gamma^2 \leq kR^2$, hence $k \leq R^2/\gamma^2$. □

The convergence theorem reveals something important about linear classification: the number of mistakes is bounded by $R^2/\gamma^2$, where $\gamma$ is the margin—the minimum distance from any training point to the optimal separating hyperplane. Large margin means easy separation and fast convergence. Small margin means slow convergence. If no margin exists (data are not linearly separable), the perceptron may run forever.

Warning · Perceptron Fails for Non-Separable Data

The convergence theorem assumes linear separability. If no separating hyperplane exists, the perceptron will cycle indefinitely, never stabilizing. For non-separable data, use methods with explicit regularization—such as the support vector machine with slack variables (covered in Chapter 4) or logistic regression with $L_2$ penalty (Chapter 3)—which are guaranteed to find the best linear classifier even when perfect separation is impossible.

💡
Historical note: Rosenblatt’s 1957 perceptron is widely considered the ancestor of modern neural networks. A multi-layer network trained by backpropagation is conceptually a direct descendant: the update rule $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta y_i \mathbf{x}_i$ reappears in stochastic gradient descent for deep learning, scaled to millions of parameters across dozens of layers.
Data Science Application · Online Learning for Streaming Data

The perceptron processes one example at a time and updates immediately—this is called online learning. Online algorithms do not require storing the entire training set in memory, making them essential for streaming data (sensor readings, web clickstreams, financial ticks). Modern online learning algorithms such as Passive-Aggressive (PA) and FTRL (Follow the Regularized Leader) are direct descendants of the perceptron, with convergence guarantees even for non-separable data. In large-scale advertising systems (e.g., click-through rate prediction), online learning is the default approach because the training data is too large to store and models must adapt in real time.

✦ Chapter Summary

This chapter established the geometric and computational foundation for linear classification. We began with the observation that features define a coordinate space, and that classification amounts to partitioning that space by a decision boundary. We formalized this through decision functions—scalar-valued maps over feature space whose zero-level sets are the decision boundaries—and showed that these level sets are special cases of isosurfaces. For linear decision functions $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x} + \alpha$, the isosurface is a hyperplane, and $\mathbf{w}$ is its normal vector. When $\mathbf{w}$ is a unit vector, $f(\mathbf{x})$ equals the signed perpendicular distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to the hyperplane. Building on this geometry, we derived the centroid method—a closed-form linear classifier based on class means—and the perceptron algorithm—an iterative optimizer with a finite convergence guarantee for linearly separable data. The concepts of overfitting, validation, and the tension between decision-boundary complexity and generalization were introduced and will be central to every subsequent chapter.

FEATURE SPACE

The feature space $\mathbb{R}^d$ is the geometric arena for classification. Each sample point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ encodes $d$ features; the label $y$ is separate. $n$ = number of training points; $d$ = dimension. Proximity in feature space approximates similarity in label.

DECISION FUNCTION

A decision function $f:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ maps every feature vector to a score. Prediction is class $\mathcal{C}$ iff $f(\mathbf{x}) > 0$; not-$\mathcal{C}$ otherwise. The magnitude $|f(\mathbf{x})|$ is a confidence score: large means far from the boundary.

DECISION BOUNDARY

The decision boundary is the zero-level set $\{\mathbf{x}: f(\mathbf{x})=0\}$. It separates feature space into two half-spaces. Overfitting occurs when a complex boundary fits spurious training details; detected by elevated validation error.

ISOSURFACES

Isosurface $S_c(f) = \{\mathbf{x}: f(\mathbf{x})=c\}$ is generically a $(d-1)$-dimensional surface. The gradient $\nabla f$ is always orthogonal to isosurfaces. Non-zero isosurfaces encode classifier confidence.

HYPERPLANE

The zero-level set of $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\alpha$ is a hyperplane: flat, $(d-1)$-dimensional, infinite. It divides $\mathbb{R}^d$ into two half-spaces. Hyperplanes generalize lines ($d=2$) and planes ($d=3$).

NORMAL VECTOR

$\mathbf{w}$ is normal (perpendicular) to $\mathcal{H}$: for any $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in \mathcal{H}$, $\mathbf{w} \cdot (\mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x}) = 0$. Changing $\mathbf{w}$ rotates $\mathcal{H}$; changing $\alpha$ translates it. This follows directly from the fact that $\nabla f = \mathbf{w}$ is constant.

SIGNED DISTANCE

When $\|\mathbf{w}\|=1$: $f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{x}+\alpha$ is the signed distance from $\mathbf{x}$ to $\mathcal{H}$. Magnitude = distance; sign = which side. Distance from origin = $|\alpha|$. For non-unit $\mathbf{w}$: divide by $\|\mathbf{w}\|$.

CENTROID METHOD

Set $\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}} - \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$, $\alpha = -\mathbf{w} \cdot (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}}+\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}})/2$. The boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the inter-centroid segment. Closed-form; no optimization needed. Optimal under equal-covariance Gaussians.

PERCEPTRON LOSS

$\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w},\alpha) = \sum_{\text{mis}} (-y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i))$. Piecewise linear, non-negative; zero iff all points correct. The update rule $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} + \eta y_i \mathbf{x}_i$ is stochastic gradient descent on this loss.

CONVERGENCE

For linearly separable data with margin $\gamma$ and radius $R$, the perceptron makes $\leq R^2/\gamma^2$ mistakes—a finite bound independent of $n$. Large margin $\Rightarrow$ fast convergence. Non-separable data: may not terminate; use SVM or logistic regression.

Exercises

Exercise 1.1  ·  HYPERPLANE GEOMETRY
Encoding a Linear Classifier for Spam Detection

A simple email spam filter uses two features: $x_1$ = number of exclamation marks and $x_2$ = number of dollar signs. The classifier uses decision function $f(x_1, x_2) = 2x_1 + 3x_2 - 6$.

  1. Describe the hyperplane. Write the equation of $\mathcal{H}$ explicitly. What is the dimension of $\mathcal{H}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$? Find two distinct points on $\mathcal{H}$ and verify they satisfy the boundary equation.
  2. Normal vector and distance. Identify $\mathbf{w}$ and compute $\|\mathbf{w}\|$. Find the unit normal $\hat{\mathbf{w}}$ and normalized bias $\hat{\alpha}$. Compute the signed distance from the email $(x_1, x_2) = (5, 3)^\top$ to $\mathcal{H}$.
  3. Interpretation. Which side of $\mathcal{H}$ is predicted as spam? For the email $(1, 1)^\top$: what does the classifier predict, how far is the email from the boundary, and is this a high-confidence prediction?
  4. Scaling and data science. A teammate proposes using $g(x_1, x_2) = 20x_1 + 30x_2 - 60$ (all coefficients multiplied by 10). Does this change (i) the predicted class for any email? (ii) the signed distance to $\mathcal{H}$? (iii) the decision boundary? Justify each answer mathematically. What practical implication does this have for feature scaling in linear classifiers?
Exercise 1.2  ·  CENTROID METHOD
Medical Diagnosis: Centroid Classifier for Tumor Classification

A dataset of tumor biopsies uses two standardized features: $x_1$ = mean cell radius, $x_2$ = mean cell texture. Training data: 4 malignant ($\mathcal{C}$): $(1,3), (2,2), (3,4), (2,3)$; 4 benign ($\overline{\mathcal{C}}$): $(-2,-1), (-1,-2), (-3,-1), (-2,-3)$.

  1. Compute centroids. Calculate $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\overline{\mathcal{C}}}$ exactly. Show all arithmetic.
  2. Derive the classifier. Compute $\mathbf{w}$ and $\alpha$. Write $f(\mathbf{x})$ explicitly. Verify $f(\mathbf{m}) = 0$ where $\mathbf{m}$ is the midpoint of the two centroids.
  3. Evaluate and interpret. Classify the new biopsy $\mathbf{x} = (0, 1)^\top$. Compute its signed distance to $\mathcal{H}$. Does the centroid method commit any training errors on this dataset?
  4. Limitation. Suppose both classes follow Gaussians with the same mean but different covariance matrices. Would the centroid method remain optimal? What would a better decision boundary look like, and which algorithm (covered later in the course) would be appropriate?
Exercise 1.3  ·  PERCEPTRON ALGORITHM
Tracing the Perceptron on a 1D Linearly Separable Dataset

Three 1D training points: $(x_1, y_1)=(1,+1)$, $(x_2,y_2)=(3,+1)$, $(x_3,y_3)=(-2,-1)$. Initialize $w=0$, $\alpha=0$, learning rate $\eta=1$.

  1. Trace the algorithm. Process points in order $1,2,3,1,2,3,\ldots$ At each step: compute $f(x_i) = wx_i + \alpha$, check classification, apply update if misclassified. Halt when all three points are correct in one full pass. Record $(w, \alpha, \mathcal{L})$ after each update.
  2. Decision boundary. What is the final decision boundary (value of $x$ where $f(x)=0$)? Is this the unique separating threshold, or are there others?
  3. Convergence bound. Using the Novikoff theorem, compute the margin $\gamma$ achieved by your final $(w^*, \alpha^*)$ (after normalizing) and the radius $R$. What is the theoretical bound $R^2/\gamma^2$? Compare to actual mistakes made.
  4. Practical limitation. Name one modification to the perceptron that addresses non-separability while retaining the online update structure, and briefly describe its key idea.
Exercise 1.4  ·  ISOSURFACES AND DECISION FUNCTIONS
Anomaly Detection via Non-Linear Decision Function

An anomaly detector uses $f(\mathbf{x}) = x_1^2 + 4x_2^2 - 9$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Readings with $f \leq 0$ are normal; $f > 0$ are anomalies.

  1. Decision boundary shape. Identify the geometric shape of $\mathcal{H} = \{f = 0\}$ and give its semi-axes. Is this a linear classifier? Justify using the definition of a hyperplane.
  2. Isosurface family. Describe $S_c(f)$ for general $c > -9$. For which values of $c$ does $S_c(f) = \emptyset$?
  3. Gradient and confidence. Compute $\nabla f(\mathbf{x})$. Verify at $\mathbf{x}_0 = (3, 0)^\top$ (on the boundary) that $\nabla f(\mathbf{x}_0)$ is orthogonal to the boundary curve. Does moving in the $\nabla f$ direction increase or decrease the anomaly prediction confidence?
  4. Neural networks connection. A neural network’s penultimate layer produces $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^k$, and the final layer applies $f(\mathbf{z}) = \mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{z} + \alpha$. Why is the decision boundary a hyperplane in $\mathbf{z}$-space even though the mapping $\mathbf{x} \mapsto \mathbf{z}$ is nonlinear? What does this imply about neural network expressiveness?
Exercise 1.5  ·  OVERFITTING AND MODEL SELECTION
Selecting Decision Boundary Complexity for MNIST Digit Classification

You classify $28 \times 28$ images ($d=784$) as "1" vs "7" from MNIST, using three classifiers: linear (hyperplane), degree-2 polynomial, degree-15 polynomial. Training errors: $2\%, 0.5\%, 0\%$. Validation errors: $3\%, 2.5\%, 12\%$.

  1. Diagnose each model. Which classifier overfits? Which underfits (if any)? Which would you choose, and why? Use the training and validation errors to justify your answer.
  2. Bias-variance in words. Describe the "bias" and "variance" of each of the three models in plain language. How does increasing model complexity affect each?
  3. Effect of sample size. If training set size doubles from $n=1000$ to $n=2000$, for which of the three models would you expect the most improvement in validation error? Justify in terms of model complexity, sample size, and overfitting.
  4. Practical protocol. Describe the complete model selection protocol you would follow—from raw data to final model—to avoid using test information during selection. Include the roles of a held-out validation set and cross-validation.
